extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students/scholars of humor and psychoanalysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative/creative criteria for jokes from Freud's Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious (1905): techniques, functions, and sources of pleasure according to a psychoanalytic/social lens. Useful for analyzing or composing jokes with Freudian concerns in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation: occurs when one creates a joke out of two words (e.g., combining 'millionaire' and 'familiar' to make 'famillionairely').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud gives this as a technique for joke-creation; the page offers the explicit example of a blended word as a condensation device. Use of portmanteau/word-blend can produce humorous effect by collapsing two ideas into one compressed signifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / Economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes tend to be short; there is a great tendency towards economy when people try to create jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize succinctness—short form concentrates the effect. The page treats shortness as a common structural feature rather than an accidental property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes as catharsis for repressed sexual and hostile energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and jokes are a form of catharsis for stored-up sexual and hostile energy arising from repression; people laugh to get rid of pent up energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud frames the joke's function as releasing psychic energy. The page notes this is his central claim (including that 'all aspects of the joke including the laughter are a catharsis'), but also records criticisms (e.g., Freud does not explain how the energy is stored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of taboo / circumvention of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes bring into the open things that might otherwise be considered taboo in a particular society and allow expression of aggression or hostility (e.g., about an ethnicity) that could not be expressed without punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud treats jokes as a way for the mind to 'find work around' for nasty, repressed emotions—jokes permit taboo expression in a socially tolerable form. When evaluating or crafting a joke, consider whether it permits forbidden content to be aired safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of pleasure: recognition, appreciation, and play
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides catharsis, Freud suggests recognition, appreciation, and play pleasures may be sources of pleasure in a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are complementary mechanisms—pleasure can come from recognizing the target, from social appreciation (audience response), or from playfulness of form/content. Use these categories to analyze why an audience finds a joke pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social cohesion / group function
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes play an important part in creating cohesion in society; they are often told in groups and serve as a way of dealing with societal aggression and diffusing tension to ensure social survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud emphasizes the communal aspect (e.g., roasts show how societies release pent-up emotions in a way that preserves social bonds). Evaluate jokes for their role in bonding, policing norms, or managing collective hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious / dream-work analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The same processes that relate to the creation of dreams in the unconscious mind are also at play when making jokes; jokes originate in the subconscious like dreams and express repressed or unfulfilled desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dream-work analogies (displacement, condensation, symbolic expression) to interpret joke formation and meaning: jokes may 'come from nowhere' in consciousness but reflect deeper psychic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of joke techniques and themes (e.g., caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud gives a detailed analysis of themes used in creating jokes, for instance he discusses caricatures as a theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing jokes, identify recurring thematic devices (caricature, irony, parody, etc.) and consider how they function within Freud's taxonomy. The page indicates Freud attempts a systematic classification of techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes as play / playful origin (Kuno Fischer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preexisting theory examined by Freud: jokes originate from man's playful nature (Kuno Fischer's view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rival criterion treats playfulness itself as the core origin/quality of jokes—evaluate whether a joke primarily functions as play rather than catharsis or social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes as metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Another preexisting theory Freud reviews: jokes may be a form of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke operates by metaphorical substitution (one idea standing in for another) and whether that mechanism produces the comic effect; Freud reviews such views as part of his broader analysis.
